title: Two Concepts of Educational Liberty
author: Daniel Buck
summary: Daniel Buck confronts a paradox at the heart of schooling, especially classical schooling: institutions that promise to form free, self-governing people constantly tell children where to sit, when to speak, and what to memorize. He resolves it with Isaiah Berlin's 'Two Concepts of Liberty.' Negative liberty, freedom from interference, is not the telos of a classroom, where knowledge, virtue, and excellence are the ends and even small disruptions harm every student's learning. Positive liberty, the capacity to direct one's own affairs, is what education actually expands, as Berlin's examples of the actor memorizing lines and the pianist drilling scales illustrate: short-term constraint purchases long-term freedom of action. Buck then takes seriously Berlin's warning that positive liberty can justify coercion 'for your own good,' cautioning teachers against using formation as cover for indoctrination or personal whims. He argues schools differ from states because their ends are discrete, teachers know their students closely, and literacy and numeracy are defensible goods, concluding that paternalism and freedom are a tension to be managed rather than solved.
points: Buck applies Berlin's negative liberty to argue that classrooms must shrink students' zone of non-interference because even minor noise impairs everyone's learning.
The actor and pianist examples show how accepting constraint in the short term expands positive liberty, the ability to do things one could not otherwise do.
Memorizing math facts and practicing quiet recitation are framed as trades of present freedom for access to literature, mathematics, and self-government.
He heeds Berlin's warning that 'forming the free person' can license coercion, urging teachers not to smuggle in political beliefs or therapeutic ideas of the self.
School paternalism is more defensible than state paternalism because schools have discrete ends, teachers know individual children, and children are not yet autonomous adults.
quotes: Schools promise to help students think and act for themselves and yet constantly tell them where to sit and how to act. How can we make sense of this paradox? Especially in classical schools, how can we presume to provide an education designed to create free citizens while telling kids to sit down, be quiet, and memorize what we tell them to?

Within the school walls, liberty is neither the final telos nor a particularly effective means to achieving it. Rather, knowledge, virtue, and excellence are primary ends. In fact, a high degree of negative liberty can work in opposition to those ends.

Things are a little different in the classroom. Even a small amount of chatter or noise can disrupt every other student’s ability to learn. When it comes to an educational institution, it is necessary to create a smaller realm of “non-interference” around students in order to achieve the end goal of learning.

Thespians spend hours memorizing their lines and practicing their delivery. That they have learned to work within the constraints of a set play does not impede their liberty in the long run. Rather, in limiting themselves for a time, it expands their positive liberty.

The same dynamic—a short-term constraint on negative liberty in exchange for a long-term expansion of positive liberty—applies to all educational endeavors. A student acquiesces to quiet and recitation, so that they might learn to read and thereby access the entire corpus of Western literature. Students commit their math facts to memory and drill algorithms so that they can create the building and structures of their society. Education gives students knowledge and abilities, making reflective choice and self-command more possible. It prepares them to govern themselves.

Forming the free person” can become a warrant for coercion when educators claim privileged knowledge of a child’s true self. “For your own good” can quickly become a justification for enforcing the petty whims and desires of the educator, not the good of the student. Teachers must be wary that teaching children to “control their passions” does not create a permission structure to indoctrinate their own political beliefs or pass along their own therapeutic conception of the self. There’s a fine line between teaching and indoctrinating, but it’s a line we can and must define.

Schools, though, are discrete institutions with discrete ends. They exist, unlike legal frameworks, not to create a general societal framework that allows pluralism and individual choice, but to direct specific students to specific lessons. Some amount of paternalism is requisite. Moreover, teachers possess more proximate knowledge of each child, children themselves are not fully autonomous adults, and reading and numeracy are more defensible ends than a comprehensive political vision of the good life.

Ultimately, we must remember that a true classical education is one that emancipates a student’s mind from provincialism, assumed ideological consensus, passions, and their own insular interests to instead direct them towards virtue and truth. But genuine virtue requires the freedom of will to choose. And that is the reality we must remember not only to prevent a needful paternalism from metastisizing into authoritarianism, but also to ensure that students leave our building as self-governing individuals, recipients of a true liberal education.
